Verified Mapping a caller address to its function by nearest known start below misattributed one call site whose real enclosing function had no known start; every high-confidence name was therefore re-checked against vtable stamps, slot agreement or callee fingerprints instead of trusting caller labels alone.

Inferred Callees in the encrypted low code region disassemble as garbage statically, so the few names depending on them rest on call shape and sibling comparison; the checker sees them decrypted at run time.

entry.title: Three small traps from one input batch: dead stack reads, erased signedness, writes past the frame
entry.summary: Seventeen of eighteen small input-layer functions verified first try or after a short diagnosis; the three things that bit are all worth knowing before touching similar functions.
entry.content:
Seventeen of eighteen small input-layer functions verified first try or after a short diagnosis; the three things that bit are all worth knowing before touching similar functions.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of eighteen small neighbouring input-layer functions and prove each against the original with the checker, one contract and one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified A function that reads an uninitialised stack word cannot be matched by reading your own stack slot: the compiler allocates a small slot with a push of a register, so the read returns the incoming register value, not the fill. The shipped rewrite stores the fill value with the proof explicitly limited to a uniform fill.

Verified A double modulo in one function provably erases signedness: reducing mod sixteen, subtracting from sixteen and reducing again gives the same result for signed and unsigned first reductions, so an unsigned-remainder mutant passed. Only the later signed division is observable, and its mutant fails. The rewrite documents which operation's signedness matters.

Verified Scripted callee writes past the end of a stack struct silently overwrite the return address and crash the original side with a zero instruction pointer. The fix is keeping every written word inside the real struct; a marker trace with distinctive words pinpoints each landing slot within minutes.

Verified Two smaller points: a zero-argument callee macro call needs a trailing comma to compile, and a thiscall callee's frame pointer is excluded from call comparison by giving it an empty register list while snapshots observe the pointed-to words.

What was decided or recommended

When a multi-call contract fails beyond the visible log prefix, trace with marker values before re-reading the code. When a function reads its own unwritten stack, prove the fill value and say so rather than mimicking the read. Deferred the one guard function whose conditional target is a large multi-call routine, for a large-function lane.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker: the residue function passes a thousand trials under a zero stack fill with the store-skipping mutant caught; the hook builder passes with fault parity on the null-allocator path and the unsigned-division mutant caught; the five-callee dispatch function passes with snapshots and downstream call arguments observing every live struct word.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three separate frame-address arithmetic slips on the five-callee function each looked like a checker defect in turn (a crash, a mystery value, a one-word mismatch) and each turned out to be my offset. The marker trace found all three. The unsigned-remainder mutant passing was briefly alarming until the residue-class argument showed it must pass.

entry.title: What the checker still could not do, and a candidate that can
entry.summary: A candidate seventh checker version now proves four shapes of function the stock checker had to defer: guards ending in a conditional jump to another routine, helpers taking a float on the float stack, call loops past the log cap, and vector registers of which only the low float matters. All four are proven by new self-test contracts, and the full existing suite gives identical verdicts.
entry.content:
A candidate seventh checker version now proves four shapes of function the stock checker had to defer: guards ending in a conditional jump to another routine, helpers taking a float on the float stack, call loops past the log cap, and vector registers of which only the low float matters. All four are proven by new self-test contracts, and the full existing suite gives identical verdicts.

What was asked

Give the checker the abilities whose absence is deferring functions: patching conditional tail jumps, observing float-stack call arguments, comparing call logs past the 1,024-call cap, narrowing a vector-register comparison to four bytes, and four reported defects. Each ability had to be an opt-in contract option that leaves every existing verdict unchanged.

What was found

Verified All four abilities are built, each with a passing rewrite, a caught wrong version, and a negative contract showing the option does the work. Ten new proof contracts run green, and 66 worker unit tests pass.

Verified Two reported defects were real and are fixed: an unknown return kind silently fell back to a 32-bit integer, and an unknown word-spec key silently resolved to random bits. Both now refuse the contract with a message, and none of the tracked contracts trip either refusal.

Verified Two deferred-function groups need no new ability. The computed tail jumps that pop the caller's word balance with the existing convention mechanism, and the vector-upper-byte case no longer reproduces on the current worker.

Inferred The remaining two defect reports could not be confirmed: no silent sequence-skew mechanism exists in the current worker, and out-of-range heap reads are a contract bug rather than a checker defect. Nothing was changed for either.

What was decided or recommended

The candidate is ready for coordinator review and install as a worker, driver, proofs and contracts change; the runtime crate rewrites build against is untouched. The recorded verdicts predate the current driver and should be re-recorded at install time. None of the deferred functions is one option away from passing: most lack any rewrite or contract, one needs re-contracting at its true location, and one is blocked by a separate one-bit float divergence.

How to reproduce it

Build the candidate worker and proofs from the lane's tree copy, run the ten proof contracts and confirm the battery script reports green, then run the tracked contracts with stock and candidate workers and confirm the pairwise comparison reports no differences.

What was confusing or went wrong

The digest's first accumulator slots collided with trampoline scratch space that looked free in the assignment list; the verdict detail shows only three calls, which hid the real failing call twice; and three lane verdicts turned out to run the wrong bytes through dropped address digits. Each is recorded in the lane report with the fix.

entry.title: Naming one hundred fifty NaturalMotion task functions
entry.summary: Verified A batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be the whole NaturalMotion ped-task system, and every one is now named: one hundred twenty at high confidence and thirty at medium, with none left blank.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be the whole NaturalMotion ped-task system, and every one is now named: one hundred twenty at high confidence and thirty at medium, with none left blank.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function from strings, imports, callers, class tables and behavior. No rewriting and no checker in this lane, only names with confidence levels.

What was found

Verified The group is the Euphoria task family: the NaturalMotion base task, its thirteen leaf behaviors such as balance, brace, flinch and shot, the blend-from-NM task, the complex NM task, and their shared helpers.

Verified The base task's per-frame method orchestrates the three behavior slots: the first run stops all behaviors and runs the start slot, later runs run the sustain slot and then the finish slot. This pins down what each slot means.

Verified Tasks request transitions by stamping a marker word holding the next task's id plus a stage byte, and a complex owner task was found testing that marker before creating its next sub-task.

Inferred The complex NM task's id getter returns a task id that was not in the id table, so it is a newly recorded id.

Verified Six constant-fill functions are default parameter rows for six behaviors, matched to their consumers by table base and row stride. Two widely called helpers turned out to be a plain memory comparison and the compiler's stack probe, not NM logic.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name the three behavior slots start, sustain and finish consistently across all leaves.
  • Name shared folded bodies once, noting every class whose table points at them.
  • Add the newly found complex NM task id to the task id table.
  • Correct the verified brace start-slot comment that calls it a per-frame update; it runs on first and retriggered processing.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch through the mapped executable image, validating the mapping by decoding one known id getter end to end. Collect callees, imports, referenced strings and constants per function, then scan the code section for direct callers of every batch member to name helpers by who calls them. Cross-check each table attribution against the per-class slot maps and read the verified rewrite notes of neighboring functions before theorizing about slot roles.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The caller counts from the decompiler-based inventory were wrong in at least three places: six initializers showed zero callers but each is called by an init loop, and a weapon helper showed one caller but has three. The function inventory also overruns one task update into its neighbor. Direct call scanning over the code section gave the true picture each time.

The two sustain slots resisted a clean distinction for a while because both build and send messages; what finally separated them was reading the base per-frame method and seeing it call one on the first run and the other afterwards.

entry.title: Two contract traps that let wrong rewrites pass, both caught by mutants
entry.summary: Verified A production batch of eighteen small memory-subsystem functions verified eighteen out of eighteen, and two of the eighteen only proved anything because each function got its own deliberately wrong version: in both cases the first wrong version passed every trial, showing the contract could not see the behaviour it claimed to check.
entry.content:
Verified A production batch of eighteen small memory-subsystem functions verified eighteen out of eighteen, and two of the eighteen only proved anything because each function got its own deliberately wrong version: in both cases the first wrong version passed every trial, showing the contract could not see the behaviour it claimed to check.

What was asked

Rewrite eighteen neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state over one thousand trials and compares return values, memory, stack, calls and faults. Every function also gets a wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified The first trap was a rotated pin pattern. One function reads a single grid cell chosen by two scripted indices, so the contract pinned thirty grid words to a shared six-value list rotated per cell. A wrong version using a different row stride passed all sixty probe trials. The shared list alternated zero and nonzero, so any two cells an even distance apart always agreed, and the stride difference was always even. Replacing the rotation with independent zero and nonzero streams per cell from a seeded random generator caught the wrong version within fifteen trials, and a second probe mutant confirmed the grid addresses were observed.

Verified The second trap was pristine-zero globals. One initialisation function writes zeros across two global ranges whose file bytes are already zero, so every write was invisible: a wrong version omitting one write passed all sixty trials. Random global fill plus a wrong version writing one instead of zero caught it within three trials.

Verified A third, smaller finding: one function flagged as calling into the encrypted first megabyte of code turned out to be checkable after all, because the call is a direct call the checker patches and scripts like any other. Nothing about the encrypted region was read or needed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Never pin a range of cells to rotations of one shared value list when a wrong address must be caught; give each cell an independent stream.
  • Always check what the pristine bytes hold before proving a function that writes constants; when they already hold the constant, fill randomly and make the wrong version write a different value.
  • Keep the per-function wrong version: both traps were invisible in the passing run and obvious the moment the wrong version passed.

How to reproduce it

Build any contract where the observable result depends only on whether a read word is zero, pin the candidate words to rotations of a zero-alternating list, and run a wrong version that reads a cell an even distance away: it passes. Replace the pins with seeded independent streams and rerun: it fails. For the globals trap, declare a range whose pristine bytes are zero, prove a zero-writing function, and run a wrong version that skips one write: it passes until the fill is randomised.

What was confusing or went wrong

The grid mutant passing sixty trials first looked like a correct proof of a wrong formula, which was briefly alarming. Reading the pin values trial by trial showed the parity alignment within minutes. The globals trap was found the same way: the passing wrong version was the signal, and checking the pristine bytes confirmed it. One further misread on a different function (a one-way copy mistaken for a swap, plus a wrong argument slot) failed loudly on the first run rather than passing quietly, which is the better failure mode.

entry.title: One configuration routine publishes uninitialized stack to a global
entry.summary: While verifying a batch of eight medium-sized routines, one of them turned out to read a stack slot it never stored and publish the block containing it to a global descriptor. The value is nondeterministic leftovers in the running game. The rewrite pins it to the harness's zero fill and notes the gap.
entry.content:
While verifying a batch of eight medium-sized routines, one of them turned out to read a stack slot it never stored and publish the block containing it to a global descriptor. The value is nondeterministic leftovers in the running game. The rewrite pins it to the harness's zero fill and notes the gap.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring routines in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares results, memory, calls and faults.

What was found

Verified All eight routines verified, one thousand trials each with no failures, and each with its own deliberately wrong version that the contract caught.

Verified In one routine's object-missing path, seven of eight descriptor words are stored and then all eight are written to the global. The eighth word is whatever the stack held at that moment. Both sides of the proof observe the harness's zero fill there, so the proof holds, but the game itself would publish a nondeterministic value.

Unknown Whether any consumer reads that word when the object is missing, which decides whether the quirk is benign or a real defect.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite documents the pinned word and the proof records it as narrowed. A follow-up lane should read the consumer of that descriptor to settle the impact. Nothing about the checker needs to change: zero-filling uninitialized stack is already its documented behaviour for exactly this case.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the sink-configuration routine in the batch, take the path where its object global is null, and count the stored words against the eight published to the descriptor global. The project's lane report names the routine and the contract that pins the word.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three of my own mistakes were caught by the checker rather than by reading: a chain-walk condition with the branches backwards, a call result threaded from the wrong register, and a callee argument count off by one because a push sat three instructions above its call. The last one showed up as the original returning into a saved register value, which the register dump at the fault made obvious. Each took one fix and one re-run.

entry.title: Naming a run of task functions: slots, vtable readback and verified callers
entry.summary: All 150 functions in the batch were named, about half from vtable slot conventions and constructor shapes and the rest from disassembly with caller checks. The reliable signals were the virtual table slot, the vtable a constructor stores, and callers confirmed by byte search; strings and imports helped nowhere in this batch.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in the batch were named, about half from vtable slot conventions and constructor shapes and the rest from disassembly with caller checks. The reliable signals were the virtual table slot, the vtable a constructor stores, and callers confirmed by byte search; strings and imports helped nowhere in this batch.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions from the ped task region, with a confidence for each. The batch covers death and injury tasks, melee tasks with many small helpers, fall and get-up tasks, seek and follow tasks, and a factory plus a family of NaturalMotion task constructors.

What was found

Verified Joining every earlier naming lane against the inventory gives a near-unanimous slot table: slot 1 is clone, slot 3 returns the constant task id, slot 5 is make abortable, simple slot 17 is per-tick processing, and complex slots 18, 19 and 20 are create next, create first and control subtask. Slot 6 returns a float urgency. Slot 7 has two shapes at one slot: movement tasks copy a target point to the caller, while death and scenario tasks allocate a dummy task object.

Verified Constructors identify themselves twice: they store their class vtable after calling the base constructor, and the stored vtable can be read back through the symbol tables to confirm the class. This named over twenty constructors and destructors, including a full family of NaturalMotion ctors sharing one abstract base.

Verified Several follow and fall tasks build subtasks through small by-id factory helpers that switch on a task id constant, and one such helper was inventoried with size zero while being a real function.

Inferred The melee task keeps its state in three flag bytes tested by a family of one-bit getters, with neighbouring values identifying the move and action-result subtask ids. One id constant could not be read because its stub sits in the encrypted range, so that id stays inferred from usage.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep the majority slot wording: get task id over get task type, and per-class names at slots 6 and 7 where behaviour genuinely differs.
  • Resolve a constructor's class by reading its stored vtable back through the symbols instead of trusting caller context alone.
  • Confirm every relied-upon caller by searching for its call bytes and resolving the true containing function; nearest-inventory attribution is frequently wrong in dense unnamed regions.
  • Treat shared tiny symbols with suspicion: one widely referenced helper labelled as a script native is the global delete operator, and two verified rewrites carry guess names that vtable readback overturns.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble through the mapped image and check the mapping against a known function first. Gather per-function calls, string references and import calls into one table, then join prior lanes against the inventory to build the slot map. For constructors, read the stored vtable and resolve its first entries. For unclear helpers, scan the code section for call bytes targeting them, verify each site reads as a real call, and attribute it through the full function inventory rather than the nearest named entry.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified One create-first function is only a few bytes long but carries an inventory size that runs into its neighbour, so linear disassembly attributed the neighbour's calls to it. Byte search contradicted the listing and the raw bytes settled it.

Verified One inventory entry spans two manager thunks plus the start of an already verified function; it was named for the thunk at its start address.

Verified The first megabyte of code is encrypted on disk, so base-class virtuals and a few stubs decode as garbage. Nothing in the batch depended on them except one task id, which was inferred instead.

entry.title: Production batch: three ui rewrites verified, one float case the checker cannot settle
entry.summary: Three input-ui functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent over a thousand trials each, and a fourth was proven halfway; the interesting result is a single input pair where the checker's original side deterministically disagrees with three independent IEEE computations, so that pair stays excluded until a real x86 machine can adjudicate it.
entry.content:
Three input-ui functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent over a thousand trials each, and a fourth was proven halfway; the interesting result is a single input pair where the checker's original side deterministically disagrees with three independent IEEE computations, so that pair stays excluded until a real x86 machine can adjudicate it.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original through the project's differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified A brightness-update function rounds through a magic-constant sequence (scale, add and subtract a large power of two, then a sign-dependent correction). With one input pair the scaled value lands exactly on a whole number, and there the original side answers one higher than every IEEE computation: exact rational arithmetic, correctly-rounded emulation, and an intrinsic-by-intrinsic replication of the same instruction sequence run on the same machine all agree with the rewrite. The split is stable across repeated identical trials, and a sweep of neighbouring inputs agrees everywhere except that exact point.

Verified The usual suspects were cleared one by one: the comparison instruction itself behaves correctly on zeros in a micro-test, both sides run with the default control word, and a second exact landing elsewhere does not diverge. The mechanism is still unknown, and it is contradiction-shaped: same emulator, same control word, same instructions, different answer.

Verified In the largest batch function, a color-helper call after two ordered float comparisons is dead code: the first test passes only if the blend exceeds the lookup, the second only if the lookup exceeds the blend, which cannot both hold. The contract leaves that call unpatched and relies on the checker's undeclared-write detection to shout if the analysis is ever wrong.

Verified A gate helper that two call sites invoke with no register setup takes no arguments; treating it as taking the leftover register value fails because the interception stub clobbers it. Checking sibling call sites settled the convention.

What was decided or recommended

  • The rewrite is IEEE-correct, so the single diverging input pair is excluded from the contract and recorded as narrowing, with a same-path replacement pair covering the same branch. A real-x86 re-run should restore the excluded pair first.
  • Lanes writing float-steering inputs should keep scaled values away from exact integers unless they are specifically testing the rounding boundary, and should verify per-trial paths rather than branch-shape counts, because distinct paths can share one call shape.
  • The half-proven large function continues from a staged retry kit: the passing entry stage plus a step-by-step plan for its loops and indirect calls.

How to reproduce it

Steer any rounding-magic sequence to an exact-integer landing with a zero residual and compare the worker's original side against a correctly-rounded emulation of the same operations; sweep the steering input across the boundary to confirm the divergence is confined to the exact point. The lane's scratch folder holds the sweep and stability scripts, the intrinsic replication probe, and the staged retry kit.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probes failed on two unforced errors: hand-computed global addresses with a wrong high digit, and a two-argument call with the arguments swapped (the last value pushed is the first argument). Both are now machine-checked habits: addresses come from a script, and every multi-argument call is verified against push order. The deeper confusion was a frame-slot mis-trace that made a live code path look dead and a dead one look live; recomputing the stack pointer at every frame reference fixed it, and the corrected reading is what proved the color-helper path genuinely dead.

entry.title: Naming ped movement, blend and frag functions
entry.summary: One hundred seventeen of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the batch exposed a slot-label trap every future naming lane should know: for move-task classes with two virtual tables, the same slot label names two different functions.
entry.content:
One hundred seventeen of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the batch exposed a slot-label trap every future naming lane should know: for move-task classes with two virtual tables, the same slot label names two different functions.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, mostly from ped movement tasks, the on-foot movement blender, fragment physics instances and injury and death tasks. Only names, no rewrites.

What was found

Verified Move-task classes with two virtual tables reuse the same slot label in the inventory for a primary-table slot and a secondary-table slot. A prior lane correctly named the primary slot as clone while this batch held the secondary slot, a float setter, under the identical label. Slot numbers alone cannot name these classes.

Verified The ninth virtual slot of move tasks sets the target point, copying a position plus flags and, in one class, forwarding the update to its movement subtask after a task-type check. The fourth slot of the timed go-to-point task debits elapsed time when its subtask is unfinished.

Verified The movement blender's table base, a factory that builds the player on-foot task, its constructor and base destructor, and the feedback-interface constructor and destructors were all resolved by reading virtual tables and constructor call chains.

Verified Recurring families were named once and applied to each member: phase blend weights, blend slot id remapping, fragment subtree masking, per-type registry setup, attach-state updates, and four byte-identical feedback dispatchers that differ only in which virtual they call.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established project slot conventions for task cloning and subtask phases, extended with target-point setting for slot nine. Thirty-three functions were left unnamed with the reason recorded, most of them bare getters to unlabeled fields or gated forwards to unknown base operations. The next naming lane in physics or animation should disassemble before trusting any slot label on a multiple-inheritance class, and should resolve constructor tables first since one table read names several functions.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped executable image, collect its direct calls, imported calls and referenced strings into one table, resolve callee names against the merged project symbols and prior lane names, scan the code section for exact callers of unnamed functions, and read virtual-table slots to tie constructors and destructors to their classes. Short functions were read in full and large ones skimmed by call list and structure.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two inventory sizes were wrong: one clone overruns into its neighbour and two functions were listed with size zero, so reads had to be checked against padding bytes. Peeking at arbitrary mid-function offsets produced garbage disassembly twice before all reads were re-anchored to function entries. A few caller attributions resolve to a named function that merely precedes the true unnamed caller, and those are marked approximate in the report.

entry.title: Naming the movement-task function group
entry.summary: One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, which turned out to be almost entirely the pedestrian movement-task code: go-to-point, route following, wandering, formation, crowd, and related task classes.

What was found

Verified The task virtual-table slots have stable meanings across classes: slot one clones, slot three returns the task id constant, slot five makes the task abortable, and slots eighteen through twenty manage subtasks (create first, create next, control).

Verified Movement tasks carry a second thirteen-slot interface table whose slots the inventory labels do not distinguish from primary slots. Its slot seven copies the target point to an out-param, slot eight reads a per-task float with a slot-ten setter, and slot six holds per-class readiness checks. Every batch entry in these slots was assigned to the correct table by comparing table base addresses.

Verified Simple movement tasks run their per-tick update through slot twenty, which calls slots twenty-two and twenty-three to refresh speed and heading; the slot-seventeen process wrapper calls slot twenty first. One code stub is shared by address between a movement task and several UI layout classes through duplicate folding, with unrelated meanings on each side.

Verified Sixteen functions are non-virtual helpers. Caller analysis attributed twelve to a single owning class, mostly subtask factories used only by one task's create-first, create-next, and control methods.

Inferred The secondary slot-eight float behaves like a per-task arrival radius, with tight values for cover movement, loose values for road crossing, and a unit default for tracking, but no direct consumer was observed.

Unknown One area-search predicate matching model category three could not be named because the meaning of that model category is not established.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named one hundred twenty functions at high confidence from slot contracts, verified rewrites, and vtable proof, and twenty-nine at medium from fully read behaviour with project-style wording.
  • Future naming lanes over movement classes should verify the vtable base address for slots six through eight instead of trusting the slot label alone, since primary and secondary slots share numbering.
  • Caller attribution by nearest symbol should be treated as a hint only; two helpers in this batch belonged to unnamed functions immediately after the attributed one.

How to reproduce it

Re-run the lane's evidence gatherer (disassembly plus string, import, and named-callee collection for every batch function), the vtable scan (pointer scan of read-only data validated against runtime type records), and the whole-text caller scan from the lane scratch folder, then compare each function's slot and callers against the contracts above.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first version of the vtable scan found nothing because type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, and because the type-name prefix contains a literal question mark the matching pattern dropped. Both were fixed and the scan then confirmed one hundred thirty-four functions with no mismatches. Two script-native labels on facing helpers look wrong (vector arguments, float results) and were treated as math helpers instead.

entry.title: One table builder verified, and the compiler hides spills inside push sequences
entry.summary: A 1,672-byte input table builder with twelve call sites verified over one thousand trials with zero failures, and the work found a spill pattern other lanes should look for: this compiler stores table pointers into dead argument slots in the middle of pushing another call's arguments, where the writes land above the stack pointer and are easy to miss. Two misread stack offsets each built a self-consistent false theory of wild reads that cost real time; both broke the moment a varying input failed to move the supposedly dependent value.
entry.content:
A 1,672-byte input table builder with twelve call sites verified over one thousand trials with zero failures, and the work found a spill pattern other lanes should look for: this compiler stores table pointers into dead argument slots in the middle of pushing another call's arguments, where the writes land above the stack pointer and are easy to miss. Two misread stack offsets each built a self-consistent false theory of wild reads that cost real time; both broke the moment a varying input failed to move the supposedly dependent value.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring input interface functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, at least one thousand trials each, with one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

  • Verified The smaller function verified 1000/1000 with zero failures, bit-exact floats, thirteen branch shapes, all eight callees firing, and its wrong version caught. Most trials complete; a minority fault identically on both sides when a record counter nears its cap.
  • Verified While pushing one call's arguments the original stores three table pointers into the dead slots of its own earlier integer arguments, plus a byte offset and a counter into two more. The inner loop then reads tables where a naive read sees dead arguments and uninitialised stack. The stack comparison stays off for this function and every stored value is observed through call arguments or globals instead.
  • Verified Rust integer division by zero raises a different fault code than the original's divide instruction (a language exception versus a divide error), so zero divisors are excluded from the contract and recorded as a narrowing. Quotient overflow is unreachable because the dividends are small differences.
  • Verified The larger function triaged clean: its thread-local read is the standard scriptable pattern, its four indirect calls all plant through fabricated objects, and its trailing call returns into a shared epilogue. No blocker found; it needs a longer session and a retry kit was left.

What was decided or recommended

The smaller function is recorded as verified with its narrowings stated. The larger is untouched for a fresh lane with the retry kit. Recommended for other lanes: compute every stack-relative target by machine arithmetic along each straight-line path before modelling it, and distrust any hand-tracked offset the moment a varying input fails to move the value that should depend on it. Also check push sequences for writes above the stack pointer, not just below it.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the function and emulate the stack pointer forward through each branch-free stretch, printing every stack-relative operand's target relative to the incoming frame. The three spill writes land on argument slots while a call's own arguments sit below. The contract then plants heap objects for the record buffer, cycles the two flag bytes through all three branches, cycles the record counter across its cap and both signedness edges, and keeps divisors non-zero. Pinning the entry register to heap versus null changes nothing, which confirms no entry register is read.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two transcription slips (one hex offset read as decimal, one disp byte misread) each produced a complete, confident, wrong story: wild reads through sums of pointers, branches that could never complete, a filler transport that was never needed. Each story survived several consistency checks because the checks reused the same wrong arithmetic. What finally broke them was cheap and empirical in both cases: pin a heap word and the original ignores it, sweep one input and the output never moves. About half the lane went to those two detours; the fix in each case was a few lines once seen.

entry.title: Retry lesson: re-derive every offset from the addressed bytes, even from a trusted kit
entry.summary: Verified A retry batch of two large deferred functions verified both, but the second lost most of an hour to table offsets copied from the first lane's kit without re-deriving them: flag bytes live 4 and 5 bytes past the row start, not 0x48 and 0x49, and the record qwords 8 and 0x10 past, not 0xC and 0x14. The kit's author had read an address ending 0xE48 as base-plus-0x48 when the base ends 0xE44, so every offset was 0x44 too high, and the retry's "independent" trace parroted the same error.
entry.content:
Verified A retry batch of two large deferred functions verified both, but the second lost most of an hour to table offsets copied from the first lane's kit without re-deriving them: flag bytes live 4 and 5 bytes past the row start, not 0x48 and 0x49, and the record qwords 8 and 0x10 past, not 0xC and 0x14. The kit's author had read an address ending 0xE48 as base-plus-0x48 when the base ends 0xE44, so every offset was 0x44 too high, and the retry's "independent" trace parroted the same error.

What was asked

Finish two functions an earlier production lane deferred for lack of time: a 952-byte message builder with twenty call sites, three virtual calls and a float loop, and a 2320-byte joystick classifier with a 64-step name and identifier chain plus a record-writing tail.

What was found

  • Verified The message builder verified clean: 1000 of 1000 trials, six branch shapes, all 21 callee slots fired, mutant caught through the calls comparison. Its two image constant blocks were varied per trial through read-only-data fills so the single-precision transcription is genuinely exercised rather than evaluated at all-zero constants.
  • Verified The classifier's retry kit contained three errors: the row offsets above, a claim that a register still held a string buffer at the tail when the code reloads it with the record pointer first, and an out-pointer listed as argument zero of a three-argument call when pushing order puts it at argument two. The retry caught the second two by tracing but copied the first, then spent most of an hour proving the execution "impossible" before re-subtracting the addresses.
  • Verified The classifier's unpatched string helpers cannot be called by the rewrite because the checker's anti-cheat revokes code pages under it, so the rewrite reimplements the case-insensitive and counted compares. Both were verified instruction by instruction against the helpers' own code, and case-flipped trial inputs prove the folding matches.
  • Verified A 71-entry trial rotation with a chain simulator asserting every trial hits its intended exit covers all 31 string tests, all 33 identifier members, both inline outcomes and the probe path; rotation length 71 is prime so every shorter script period decorrelates across exits.

What was decided or recommended

Both rewrites were accepted. Retry lanes should treat a previous lane's kit as unverified input and re-derive every address, offset and argument index from the bytes before building on it; a kit that is right about thirty facts still costs an hour when the thirty-first is wrong. The offset error pattern to watch for is a base address whose low digits are nonzero, where the offset must be subtracted, never read off the end of the constant.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch's two proof contracts through the version 6 driver at 1000 trials each and confirm zero failures with caught mutants; confirm the classifier's row layout by subtracting the table base from each addressed constant in its tail; and re-run the trial simulator to confirm all 70 chain trials hit their intended exits with no shadowing.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified With the wrong offsets, the globals comparison showed the same values in a different order on the two sides, which looked like the original was writing different rows or the worker was misreporting. Four debug contracts with split globals ranges narrowed it to one word before the actual cause, a 0x44 subtraction error, was spotted. Separately, an early reading of the relocation table repeated the classic double-added-base mistake and reported nothing relocated; the coordinator's reloc script is the authority.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 6 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in the entry "Hourly reviews, 5 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in the entry "Hourly reviews, 5 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:0516,048 functions verified, 42.9% of the functions and 28.6% of the code by size: 219 functions and 56,000 bytes in the hour, the best hour since the morning, with 28 lanes running. By the launcher's clock large-function lanes made 2,370 bytes per lane-hour (48 of 56 verified) and small-function lanes 2,300 (104 of 110). Direction: 141 methods of six class families are lifted with their proof in the pipeline. Trust, three results. First, the emulator question is measured. A probe with no game code ran 269 float instruction sequences on this machine and on the pipeline's real x86 runner: 24 give different result bits and 130 more differ only in status flags. The differences that matter are the float stack's precision setting being ignored for add, subtract, divide and square root, a signalling not-a-number not being quieted on a 64-bit load, the sign of the result of a masked invalid operation, and the low bits of sine, cosine and arctangent. Counted from the game's code, 85 of 38,381 game functions use those instructions and 3 of the verified ones do: the game computes in the vector instruction set and uses the float stack almost only to return values. Two of the probe's own expectations turned out wrong on real hardware (an 80-bit load does not quiet a signalling not-a-number, and a vector minimum raises the invalid flag for a quiet one), which is what running it there was for. Second, the last strengthening lane re-proved all 47 of its blind proofs and found two rewrites wrong in ways unrelated to signedness: one returned early where the original runs a second block, and one stored the wrong constant into a structure on its stack, hidden because the proof skipped the pointer to that structure and compared nothing in its place. Third, a count from the contracts: 2,992 verified functions skip an argument without observing what it points to.The probe is in the workspace and runs in the pipeline on every push; its results from real hardware are kept beside the emulator's. The 85 functions that use emulator-sensitive instructions are listed, and their proofs are to be repeated on a real x86 machine, which needs the owner's hardware. An audit lane is adding snapshots to a sample of 60 proofs that skip a pointer and counting how many tracked rewrites then fail. Coordinator commits now hold a lock the tick honours, after a tick's commit took a staged crate into a routine commit. Stop doing: treating a lane's reading of documentation as the reference when the real thing can be run; two of thirty-six expectations were wrong. The kernel pool is at 17.5 GB.
01:0516,240 functions verified, 43.4% of the functions and 29.3% of the code by size: 192 functions and 50,500 bytes in the hour at a mean of 21 lanes, with up to 31 running. Free memory, not commit headroom, is now what holds the lane count: it sat between 1.5 and 3 GB for most of the hour. By the launcher's clock small-function lanes made 2,210 bytes per lane-hour (177 of 184 verified) and large-function lanes 1,990 (27 of 37, the lowest share yet: four partly proven, three stopped by something the checker cannot do). The large functions that are left are the hard ones, and the queue of partly proven functions has grown to 59 functions and 176,000 bytes, a quarter of all deferred code. Reading the 60 deferrals filed as a checker gap showed two kinds. About half name limits that later checker versions removed (a call log of 256 calls, one scripted answer per callee) and are being retried now that queue lanes take the queues in turn; one such lane verified 28 of 29 functions deferred for stray bytes in an argument. The other half repeat four real gaps: a conditional jump out of a function, more calls in a trial than the log holds, a float handed to a callee on the float stack, and a vector argument of which four bytes mean anything. Trust: the audit of skipped arguments has its population: 2,992 verified functions skip an argument without observing what it points to, and in a sample 87% of those arguments are pointers into the function's own frame that it writes through, the kind that hid a wrong constant yesterday. Its snapshot runs on 60 of them are not finished; no wrong rewrite so far.A checker lane is briefed and queued to build the four abilities and to confirm four defects earlier lanes reported in passing, as a candidate version 7 with the same rules as version 6: every new ability an option that is off unless asked for, every existing verdict unchanged, nothing counted until the coordinator has reviewed and installed it. No change to the lane mix this hour: the difference between kinds is within what one hour's sample can show. Stop doing: nothing new this hour. Watching: free memory under 2 GB makes the machine page, and if lanes slow visibly the free-memory guard goes up, not down. Still with the owner: the kernel pool, 17.6 GB, and a real x86 machine for the 85 emulator-sensitive functions.
02:0516,394 functions verified, 43.8% of the functions and 29.9% of the code by size: 154 functions and 48,000 bytes in the hour at a mean of 24 lanes. Two faults in the process were found by reading what it produced, and both were costing work quietly. First, the production brief contradicted itself about time: its shared opening, written for one-hour survey lanes, said about 60 minutes, and its task section said 110. Of the last 87 production lanes, 11 stopped between 26 and 75 minutes with 29 functions untried, several writing that the next function needed 60 to 90 minutes when they had more than that left; one small-function lane verified 14 of 28 and stopped at 59 minutes. Second, withdrawing a rewrite forced the importer of verified rewrites to read every lane again; on a cold file cache that pass ran into the tick's 200-second limit, was stopped before it saved anything, and started again on the next tick, so nothing was imported for 23 minutes (55 functions waited; none was lost). Throughput by kind, over four hours so that the sample is large enough: queue lanes, which re-run deferred functions with guidance, 3,216 bytes per lane-hour (23 lanes, 58 of 76 functions); large-function lanes 2,354; small-function lanes 2,238. The review's numbers had no line for queue lanes until now. Trust: the audit of skipped pointer arguments measured 60 contracts with snapshots added and found one rewrite wrong (it passes a buffer of zeros to a callee that reads its input there), one suspect and 49 harmless differences; the wrong one is withdrawn. The lane that reads every such site from the original's code has classified 4,633 sites in 2,992 functions so far: 1,080 pure outputs, 416 inputs the rewrite fills the same way, 119 sites in 50 functions where the original fills a buffer and the rewrite does not (candidates, each still to be judged by what the callee does with it), and 3,018 its script cannot yet map. In this hour's own contracts, 54 skip an argument and 50 of them snapshot what it points to; the other four say why not; all 241 verified rows have a wrong version that was caught. Direction: no lift lane had run for three hours, and lifting is the only work that produces portable code.The owner set a limit of 15 lanes at 02:00 so that the laptop does not overheat; it replaces the earlier instruction to fill the memory, and the coordinator does not raise it. With 15 slots the mix decides the output, so: queue lanes go from three slots in twelve to four and small-function lanes from three to two; up to three of the 15 are kept for lift, checker and audit lanes. At this hour's rate per lane, 15 lanes verify about 30,000 bytes an hour, which puts the remaining 5.4 million bytes at about 180 hours. Brief version b19: the opening no longer names a time, and a lane does not stop while a function is untried and 25 minutes remain; if the next function is too large for the time left it proves a stage of it. A withdrawal no longer forces a full import pass (it does not need one); the cases that do (a restore, an edit to the importer or the scan) are run by the coordinator under the commit lock without a time limit, never by a tick. Queue lanes are now in the review's numbers. A lift lane is queued for the next class whose methods are all verified (a user-interface clip class and the replay progress bar, 31 methods). Stop doing: one small-function slot, and full import passes inside a tick. Health: nothing left behind by lanes; the kernel pool is at 17.8 GB and still with the owner.
03:0516,508 functions verified, 44.1% of the functions and 30.4% of the code by size: 114 functions and 35,600 bytes in the hour, at a mean of 20 lanes falling to the owner's limit of 15. By kind: large-function lanes 3,077 bytes per lane-hour (14 of 16), queue lanes 2,851 (10 of 18), small-function lanes 2,206 (92 of 95). Trust was the hour's work. The lane that read every skipped pointer argument from the original's code finished: 4,633 sites in 2,992 verified functions; 1,368 inputs the rewrite fills the same way, 1,080 pure outputs, 174 inputs the rewrite does not fill, and 2,011 its reader could not map. Of the 174 it judged 36 sites in 16 functions wrong, 30 sites in 13 functions undecidable because the callee is in the part of the code that is encrypted on disk, and 108 harmless. The coordinator checked the 16 with a separate reader for the callee side and by reading the original around the calls: two were already repaired and re-proved by the lane, five were confirmed on both sides and withdrawn, and for nine the two readings disagree or the store was not seen independently (in one the lane's reader seems to have matched the wrong local). Reading only has now been wrong in both directions in two days, once by the coordinator and here in part by a lane, so those nine are settled by a run, not by a third reading. The checker candidate is built: four abilities and two refusals, with 47 of 48 of the checker's own contracts byte-identical against stock; the coordinator read the two places where it replaces existing worker code and both are gated on the new option. Process: the queue of functions blocked by a checker gap came round three times in two hours and its lanes verified 4 of 17, each proving again that the same functions need abilities the stock checker lacks; and a queue lane's list did not record which queue it served, so the review could not see which queues repay a lane. Free memory fell to 2.1 GB with only 15 lanes: the lanes hold 4.7 GB between them and the kernel's non-paged pool holds 18.0.Two repair lanes are running on the 27 functions in question (15 judged wrong, 12 with an unreadable callee). Each rebuilds the buffer as the original does, compares the stored words from now on, and then runs the old behaviour as the wrong version: if that fails the rewrite was wrong, if it passes it was not and the earlier proof stands. A second lane that did not write the checker candidate builds it from source and runs 150 production contracts chosen by feature on both workers, with their wrong versions; the candidate is installed only if no decision and no compared value changes. The checker-gap queue is held out of the rotation until then. Queue lists now carry the queue's name. Not yet running against anything: the 2,011 sites the reader could not map, about half of which are a local reused across calls; a reader for those is the next audit lane when a slot is free. Stop doing: sending lanes to the checker-gap queue before the checker can do what they need. Nothing changed in the lane mix: one hour under the new limit is too little to judge it, and no lane on brief b19 has finished yet. Health: nothing left behind by lanes; the memory is with the owner (the service that holds the kernel pool, or a restart).
04:0516,593 functions verified, 44.4% of the functions and 30.9% of the code by size: 85 functions and 36,200 bytes in the hour at a mean of 16 lanes, against 35,600 bytes at 20 lanes the hour before, so the code verified per lane rose by a quarter. By kind: queue lanes 4,097 bytes per lane-hour, small-function lanes 3,281, large-function lanes 2,808. The nine lanes that have finished on brief b19 verified 116 of 118 functions and left none untried; the 73 lanes before it on b18 left 29. Direction is the hour's finding. 160 methods are lifted to portable Rust, 19 of them this hour, and every lift so far took a class. Measured now: 2.37 million bytes are verified, 0.71 million of them in named classes and 1.67 million in functions that belong to no class. Lifting class by class cannot reach more than three verified bytes in ten, and the coordinator had been choosing even more narrowly, only from classes verified in full (14 classes and 13,400 bytes left), where 119 classes with four or more verified methods and nothing lifted hold 110,600. Trust: both repair lanes settled the skipped-pointer question by a run. Of 27 functions examined, 17 handed a callee something other than the original does; 14 are repaired and re-proved, 3 are withdrawn with a specification of the repair, 10 were not wrong and 1 is undecided. The lane that read the sites had called 16 wrong and was right about 10; the coordinator's own second opinions on ten of them were right five times. A run settled what two rounds of reading could not. The second lane on the checker candidate found what the first could not see from 48 small contracts: the worker is sound (100 production contracts, every verdict equal), but the candidate's driver refuses 209 existing contracts, and in refusing them shows that the stock driver gives random bits to any input word whose description uses a key it does not know. 73 verified proofs ran that way: valid for the inputs they got, weaker than their contracts say. Two coordinator mistakes this hour, both caught by lanes: a lift lane was briefed for five classes that were half lifted already, because the check looked for the class's name; and a withdrawn function could have been imported again from the lane whose proof had just been withdrawn.The first lift of a group of free functions is briefed and queued ahead of the next class: 130 verified functions of the object pools, to be lifted as one owning type with methods, and its report is to say what of the class method carries over. Lift families are now chosen by verified bytes not yet lifted, from classes that need not be complete, and the census marks what is lifted by address. A lane is writing the contract each of the 73 authors meant and settling each function by a run; another is making the checker candidate a drop-in (the two refusals become a recorded warning unless a contract asks to be strict) and must show no changed decision across all 21,900 lane contracts before anything is installed. The importer now refuses a withdrawn function from the lane whose proof was withdrawn. Withdrawals are made on a run, or on a reading the coordinator has confirmed on both sides, never on a lane's reading alone. Stop doing: choosing lift work from complete classes only. The lane mix stays: queue lanes lead again and b19 is doing what it was written for. Health: nothing left behind; processor at 20% with 15 lanes; the kernel pool is at 18.2 GB and still with the owner.
05:0516,666 functions verified, 44.5% of the functions and 31.3% of the code by size: 73 functions and 31,000 bytes in the hour at a mean of 14 lanes, five of them on trust and lift work. The hour's result is in the other two columns. Lift: the first lift of functions that belong to no class worked. One lane took 130 verified object-pool routines, grouped them by the shape of the data they share, and lifted 32 of them as 14 methods on 8 owning types, with 32 differential cases passing on the 32-bit target; a second lane lifted 16 methods of a class that is not verified in full. Both are in the workspace with their proof in the pipeline. Measured for the first time: 208 verified routines now have a portable counterpart proven against them, 25,200 bytes, which is 1.1% of the 2.37 million verified bytes. The two lift lanes of this hour added 8,400 of those bytes, about 4,200 bytes per lane-hour, which is as much code per lane as verifying produces (2,200 to 4,200 by kind this hour). So lifting is not slower per lane than verifying; it has simply been given one lane in fifteen. Trust: all 73 proofs that had run on random bits hold under the contract their authors meant, on the stock checker, with a wrong version caught for each; 34 of them turned out to have been proved on private copies of the driver, which do not count, and are now proved on the stock one. Checker version 7 is installed. A third lane made the candidate a drop-in (no difference between the two validators on 22,035 lane contracts, identical inputs for the 209 it used to refuse), and the coordinator's own two regressions before the swap showed no mismatch, including the old driver with the new worker, which is what running lanes get. Process: a pipeline run failed on a lift commit whose content was sound, because the commit went out while two functions were listed as both verified and unverified. The cause, found only when a new guard refused a later commit for the same reason: a full import run by hand updates the verified half of the rewrite tree and leaves the unverified half to the next tick.Lifting gets four of the fifteen slots from now on, up from one or two, fed two at a time until the supervisor's next window, which gets a lane kind for it; the brief for a free-function group now carries the first lane's seven lessons, and lift throughput is in the review's numbers, in routines and bytes. Two more are queued: the rest of the pools and the streaming slot table. The checker-gap queue is back in the rotation now that version 7 can do what its functions need; briefs are at b20, which describes the four new options and requires strict: true in every new contract. A full import by hand now brings both halves of the rewrite tree into line, the coordinator's commit helper refuses to commit while the tree is inconsistent or holds a tick's unfinished work, and a tick step that fails writes its last lines where the five-minute status shows them (one had failed silently for 38 minutes). Stop doing: treating lift as a side lane. Not yet done: the cause of that 38-minute silent failure is still unknown, and the 377 functions with an unread skipped-pointer site are being run now by one lane that may not reach them all. Health: free memory 2.3 GB with 15 lanes, kernel pool 18.4 GB, both with the owner; processor at 34%.
06:0516,745 functions verified, 44.8% of the functions and 31.7% of the code by size: 79 functions and 35,100 bytes in the hour at a mean of 14 lanes (large-function lanes 2,848 bytes per lane-hour, queue lanes 3,043, small-function lanes 2,999). Lifted: 284 verified routines now have a portable counterpart proven in the pipeline, 30,500 bytes, 1.3% of the verified code; three lift lanes added 76 routines and 5,400 bytes this hour (a font string class, 27 more pool routines, and the streaming slot table, the second group outside any class). The routines in these groups are small, about 80 bytes each, so the hour's lift rate in bytes is half of last hour's. Trust: a routine production lane found a blind spot in the checker by doing what the brief asks. One of its deliberately wrong versions stored a result one table slot too low and passed 1,000 trials. The coordinator confirmed the cause in the worker: a changed global word is recorded as the start of its declared range and its new value, so where inside a range a write lands is not compared. 1,578 verified functions, 9.4%, have a contract of record with a range wider than one word. None is known to be wrong. The lane that ran the skipped-pointer sites nobody could read finished 335 of 377: 238 settled without repair, one wrong and repaired, 23 where the stored words differ and the callee is read as reading them first, and 28 whose proof of record did not reproduce when run unchanged or whose original never completes a trial. The first functions retried on checker version 7 from the queue that waited for it: four of six verified. Process, found by reading results: a queue lane proved thirteen stages of one large function and recorded it as not reached, as the coordinator's queue brief told it to, and the next lane was sent to the first lane's single stage and proved five of the thirteen again; and with the memory guard at 3.0 GB the lane count fell from 15 to 11 in 45 minutes although nothing was paging, because the kernel pool and other programs take up what finished lanes give back.Two audit lanes are re-running 400 of the 1,578 proofs on the stock checker with every global range split into single words, which cannot hide a misplaced write, and recording whether the function wrote a global at all; more follow according to what they find. A checker lane is making the worker record each changed word's own address, as a candidate version 8 under the same rules as version 7. Brief b21: every new contract declares its globals one word per range. The 23 skipped-pointer candidates stay in the tree, in question, and are being settled by a run, since a reading of the callee was wrong three times in thirteen last time; the 28 proofs that did not reproduce are being run exactly as recorded by a separate lane, which will say whether the audit's method or the proofs are at fault. The queue brief now records advanced work as partly proven with its stage files, and the queue builder reads a not-reached row that reports proven stages. The memory guard is 2.5 GB, as it was for two hours on 5 October, with a stop line at 1.2 GB or steady paging; it goes back to 3.0 when the kernel pool is released. Lift integration is now a script that refuses a lane whose shared code differs, merges module lists instead of overwriting them and runs the tests; its own test run caught its one mistake before a commit. The supervisor gets its lift lane kind at the 06:30 restart. Stop doing: integrating lifts by hand. Largest risk nothing runs against yet: lifted modules are proven one method at a time and are not yet assembled into anything that runs together.
07:0516,817 functions verified, 44.9% of the functions and 32.0% of the code by size: 72 functions and 19,000 bytes in the hour, about half of the hours before, at a mean of 13 lanes. The drop is allocation, not a slowdown: five or six of the thirteen lanes were on trust work and three on lifting, so only seven production lanes finished (large-function lanes 3,948 bytes per lane-hour, small-function lanes 4,447, queue lanes 2,478, all at or above their usual rates). Lifted: 312 verified routines, 36,200 bytes, 1.5% of the verified code; 28 routines and 5,700 bytes this hour from three lanes (the banked-voice layer of the audio code and two groups of large pedestrian task routines, one of them the first lift lane the supervisor started by itself). Lists of large functions chosen by name give four to seven routines a lane and lists of small ones about thirty, with about the same number of bytes either way. Trust: checker version 8 is installed. The fix for the comparison of global writes is one line in the worker (each changed word is recorded with its own address); its lane's regression on 150 production contracts and the coordinator's two regressions on the checker's own contracts showed no changed verdict except the wrong version that is supposed to fail. Before the fix, 400 of the 1,578 proofs with a wide global range were re-run with one-word ranges: 281 hold, 116 pass but never wrote a global in any trial, 3 did not reproduce for other reasons, none had a misplaced write. The 28 proofs that an audit lane could not reproduce all reproduce exactly as recorded, on the proving lanes' own libraries and on fresh builds of the tracked files; the audit's added snapshots had read through pointers that are invalid in some trials. That weakens the same audit's 23 repair candidates, which were rightly left in the tree and are being settled by a run. Direction: the project's written plan says no 64-bit work before the rewrite phase is complete, because mixing the two stalled another project's lanes, and this night a quarter of the lane starts were moved to lifting. The two are separate lanes and do not mix inside one, but it is a change of emphasis against the written plan.The remaining 1,177 proofs with a wide global range are re-run unchanged on version 8 by three lanes, which also sort the proofs that never wrote a global into functions that only read their globals and functions whose write path no trial reached. Briefs are at b22 and name version 8. Lift stays at three starts in twelve and is not raised further until the owner has said whether lifting during the rewrite phase is what he wants at that share; the question and the numbers are put to him in the chat. Lift briefs now tell lanes to write comments as they should read in the repository, and the chooser tells a lane with large functions to triage by shape and lift two or three shapes. Stop doing: re-running proofs with hand-split ranges now that the checker compares positions itself. Open: thread-local words are not compared by the checker at all (reported by the lane that made the fix); 116 proofs say nothing about their function's global writes; three proofs did not reproduce under the exact contract. Health: nothing left behind by lanes; 2.5 to 3.1 GB available with the guard at 2.5; kernel pool 18.7 GB, still with the owner; processor 24%.
08:0516,856 functions verified, 45.1% of the functions and 32.1% of the code by size: 39 functions and 9,800 bytes in the hour, a quarter of what an hour gave at midnight. Three causes, in order of size. Allocation: of 12.6 lanes on average, three were re-running old proofs on the new checker and three or four were lifting, so about six produced verified code. Memory: all 47.6 GB is in use (kernel pool 19.0 GB, the owner's programs about 19, this project about 8.6), nothing new could start for 82% of the hour, and ticks and builds run slower than at night. The work itself: the large-function lanes verified 8 of 12 and left four partly proven, at 1,530 bytes per lane-hour, half their usual rate. That last cause is the lasting one, so it was measured: 2.34 of the 5.21 million bytes still to verify are in 1,095 functions of 1,000 bytes and more. 153 functions have at some time been left partly proven in stages (412,000 bytes); 32 were finished later, 18 of them by queue lanes; and of the 121 still open, 116 have been worked on by one lane only. So the staged functions are not stuck, they are not being revisited: their queue got one queue lane in ten and grew by 30,000 bytes an hour. Lifted: 345 verified routines, 40,000 bytes, 1.6% of the verified code; 33 routines and 3,800 bytes this hour. Trust: the re-run of the proofs with a wide global range on checker version 8 has covered 1,185 of 1,578 with no misplaced write; of the 412 that never changed a global in any trial, 402 belong to functions that only read their globals and 10 write on a path no trial reached; 14 failed for another reason when run unchanged. The skipped-pointer candidates are settled: of 23, seven were wrong and are repaired, 14 were not, two are recorded with the reason. A lane left two folders of stage verdicts at the repository's root by giving the driver a relative path.Every second queue lane now goes to the functions partly proven in stages, and the other queues share the turns in between. Lift stays at three starts in twelve, not raised, until the owner answers the question put to him at 07:05. With the last audit lane finishing, the trust lanes drop from five to one or two next hour, which gives those slots back to verifying. To come when slots are free: a lane for the 10 proofs whose global write is on a path no trial reached, and an exact reproduction of the 14 proofs that failed when re-run, before anything is concluded from them (the last such batch was the audit's fault, not the proofs'). Brief b23: every tool gets an absolute path inside the lane's folder, and a lane checks for its own stray paths before it finishes; the five-minute status now lists any untracked path outside the rewrite tree. The fast guard's limit is 3 GB while memory is this tight. Stop doing: giving the largest and best-performing queue one turn in ten. Health: nothing left behind by lanes; processor 8%; memory is the constraint and its fix is the owner's (the service that holds the kernel pool, or a restart).
08:55The lanes stopped at 08:48 and none is running; this row closes the run for now. At the stop: 16,898 functions verified before the last withdrawal, 45.2% of the functions and 32.1% of the code by size; 483 verified routines lifted to portable Rust with their proof in the pipeline, up from 141 at midnight. The last 45 minutes produced the regression's first result: two lanes re-ran 700 proofs made on checker versions 1 and 2, unchanged, on version 8. 688 hold and are now recorded on the current checker; 12 do not, 1.7%, close to the 2% of the morning's sample. Eleven of the twelve are vacuous by the rule the checker has had since version 5 (in six the original never completed a trial, in five a callee never fired on a completed one), and one compared the first 256 of 320 calls. None of the twelve rewrites is known to be wrong; a function without a proof is not counted, and they were withdrawn. None of the 700 had a deliberately wrong version on file. A regression lane does 350 proofs in under half an hour, so the 12,084 older proofs still to re-run are about 30 lane-runs. Then, in this order: the two regression lanes that were queued (500 proofs each) and the regression lane kind from the supervisor's next window; the queue of twelve withdrawn functions, which has its own guidance (a contract in which the original completes its trials and every callee fires, and a wrong version); the lanes that were cut off, whose batches go back to the pool. The importer now lets any lane's proof made on the current checker bring a withdrawn function back, not only a strengthening lane's, so that queue lanes can return these. Changed in the hour: every second queue lane goes to functions partly proven in stages; the queue builder knows proofs that do not hold as their own queue.
