entry.title: A signed bound check and a silent contract hole in one batch
entry.summary: Twenty-six small table-manager routines were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent, and the batch surfaced two things worth knowing: one routine bounds its table index with a signed compare that admits very large index values, and the contract linter does not check global address ranges, so wrong ones pass silently with reduced coverage.
entry.content:
Twenty-six small table-manager routines were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent, and the batch surfaced two things worth knowing: one routine bounds its table index with a signed compare that admits very large index values, and the contract linter does not check global address ranges, so wrong ones pass silently with reduced coverage.

What was asked

Rewrite thirty small neighbouring routines from the files-memory area and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, one contract per routine, each with its own deliberately wrong version.

What was found

Verified The batch is one subsystem: two handle tables with an init, register and reset routine each, a pool table with init and find-and-mark routines, a chunk table, an object table teardown, four tick-to-float converters sharing one query helper, three fixed-field name setters, a mode dispatcher with its cache and readiness gates, two access predicates, and a few open, snapshot, shutdown and scan helpers.

Verified The handle-register routine checks its index with a signed 16-bit upper bound after a signed full-word sign check. Small and negative full-word values are rejected, but an index whose low half sits in the top half of the 16-bit range passes and addresses memory before the table, down to 256 KB below it for the largest admitted value. The rewrite keeps the behaviour and the proof covers those values; live callers presumably never pass them.

Verified One scanner routine reads its object base from entry registers whose saved slots overlap a temporary, so its behaviour depends on caller registers the checker cannot transport to a rewrite; it was deferred, not guessed at.

Verified One drain loop exits only when its callees clear a global flag, which intercepted callees cannot do, so any trial entering the loop would run to the call cap; it was deferred with the analysis recorded.

What was decided or recommended

Twenty-six routines count as verified, each over one thousand trials with branch coverage confirmed from the verdicts and a caught wrong version. The lint and schema checks should plausibility-check global address ranges: six contracts in this lane used ranges with a dropped digit, still passed, and were caught only because verdict branch shapes showed paths never taken. Seeding read-only globals is silently ignored and should either work or warn.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; every verdict records full branch shapes and a failing wrong version. The signed-bound behaviour can be re-derived by reading the index compare and the sign-extending move that follows it in the register routine. The silent-range behaviour is preserved in the lane's early probe verdicts, where two misdeclared ranges passed all comparisons.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two rewrites first failed on missed register reloads just before a return, one branch was read inverted, one multi-argument call passed its words in push order instead of argument order, and code-pointer constants had to be relocated exactly as the original's loader fixups do. Each was caught by the first probe run and fixed from the checker's first mismatch. A build file lock from a lingering scan was worked around by moving the old library aside.

entry.title: The optimizer can delete the reads a fault-parity proof needs
entry.summary: Verified A logically identical Rust rewrite of a filter-matching predicate survived memory reads the original faults on, because the compiler proved the result from the arguments alone and skipped the reads. Marking the reads volatile restored fault parity with no change in logic.
entry.content:
Verified A logically identical Rust rewrite of a filter-matching predicate survived memory reads the original faults on, because the compiler proved the result from the arguments alone and skipped the reads. Marking the reads volatile restored fault parity with no change in logic.

What was asked

Rewrite sixteen small motion-tree routines in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, outgoing calls and faults over one thousand trials each.

What was found

Verified One predicate reads its entry count from the same table it then walks, so a count of two or more re-reads the count word as an entry pointer and faults. The first rewrite transcribed the loop faithfully, yet on three trials in sixty the original faulted while the rewrite returned normally.

Verified Disassembly of the compiled rewrite showed the cause: the compiler had split the loop into several versions keyed on the argument values, and the version for arguments whose answer is always zero returned without reading a single entry. The reads were logically redundant, so removing them was a valid optimisation of the value computed, but it changed which addresses fault.

Verified Reading the entry bytes with volatile loads keeps every read in program order while still compiling to plain byte loads. After that change the rewrite passed one thousand trials with matching faults on the count-overlap trials, and a deliberately wrong version with an inverted gate failed as required.

Inferred A sibling predicate verified by an earlier lane passed with plain reads only because it takes no arguments for the compiler to split on. Any search loop whose result is fully determined by loop-invariant arguments can fall into this trap.

What was decided or recommended

  • When a pure loop shows original-faults while rewrite-returns, suspect versioned loops before suspecting the logic, and confirm by disassembling the rewrite.
  • Use volatile loads for the fault-relevant reads in such loops, with a comment saying why, rather than restructuring the logic.
  • Keep fault-parity trials (counts that re-read as pointers, short tables) in every such contract: without them the elided reads are invisible.

How to reproduce it

Build a rewrite of an entry-walking predicate whose match conditions depend only on the arguments, include trials where the count word is re-read as a pointer, and run the checker: the correct rewrite fails with the original faulting and the rewrite returning. Disassembling the rewrite shows an early-return path that reads nothing. Switching the entry-byte reads to volatile loads makes the same contract pass.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first failure looked like a logic error in the match conditions, and the conditions were rechecked twice before the compiled code was examined. The mismatch detail only said one side faulted and the other did not, which pointed at the reads rather than the branches once the faulting address (the small count value) was noticed.

entry.title: Naming the event handler and its neighbours
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering inverse kinematics, damage events, the ped event handler and movement tasks are now named, with the event virtual table slot map confirmed and extended along the way.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering inverse kinematics, damage events, the ped event handler and movement tasks are now named, with the event virtual table slot map confirmed and extended along the way.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred and fifty unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and grading each name high, medium or low confidence.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into five groups: IK solvers and managers, damage and death events with a killed-suspect orchestrator, about fifty event handler response slots, the event-group update, and movement-task constructors, destructors and clones.

Verified Joining an earlier lane's event method names to the class-analysis vtable slots pins the shared event slot meanings: type, priority, clone, update, affects-ped, subject ped and entity, supersedes, audible range, validity, takes-priority-over and clone-task. Three more slots were identified from code shape: a subject-presence test and a priority flag getter with its clearer.

Verified Each event handler slot builds a specific response task, so the constructor it calls names it: fire threats build walk-round-fire, shocking events pick one of four shocking responses, revival builds revive, and so on. Slots that only clear or forward the pending task were named for that behaviour instead.

Verified Twenty-one consecutive eight-byte functions are one pattern: secondary-vtable deleting-destructor thunks that shift the object pointer and jump to the real deleting destructor. Movement-task constructors and destructors identify their class by the vtable constants they install.

Verified Both IK manager updates first ask the windowing layer whether the game window is minimized, then step. A small entity-kind field read as bits six to nine distinguishes vehicles from peds in the subject getters.

Inferred A routine that merged symbols label as a script-native message sender is called in the memory-free position by two deleting destructors, so the label looks wrong and the routine frees memory.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred and forty-three functions were named, about two thirds at high confidence, following the established per-area conventions. Seven were left empty at low confidence: four kind-dispatched getters whose returned fields are unknown, one virtual-only IK setup helper, and two handler slots whose response-task classes have no recorded vtable. The next naming lane should identify entity-kind value six and the three unknown simple-task vtables near the jump-task family first.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image and decode one known function end to end before trusting the mapping. Gather per-function evidence first: direct callees resolved through the merged symbols, names from earlier lanes and verified rewrites, string references, vtable cross-references, and a caller scan over the code section. Resolve constructor and destructor classes through the vtable constants they install, and event slots through the response-task constructors they call.

What was confusing or went wrong

Early evidence output truncated callee lists to six entries, which hid response-task constructors and made several handler slots look task-free; printing full lists fixed a wrong theory about assessment-only slots. A few production-lane callee names turned out to be weak guesses that contradicted the code shape and had to be ignored. Two functions the inventory lists with size zero are real and were named from their code.
